title: 5 months building my momentum speedrunner with AI: my process, mistakes and lessons
author: k0zakinio
selftext:
A bit of background: my main job is web development, where I use Claude/Codex day in, day out. For the last 5 months I’ve also been building [RIDGERUNNERS](https://store.steampowered.com/app/4970370/RIDGERUNNERS/?utm_source=aigamedev), a Tribes-inspired momentum speedrunner.

I’ve always wanted a game built around Tribes-style skiing and speedrunning, and nothing quite scratched that itch. So I thought I’d give it a go myself.

Here’s the latest trailer, and a bit about how I’ve been making it, what’s worked, and what hasn’t.

**Concept**

I had a pretty strong idea of what I wanted at the start and basically beelined towards it. Within 1–2 weeks I had something that looked jank as hell, but already played like the thing I’d imagined: skiing across big landscapes, finding routes and trying to beat your time.

I uploaded it to itch and had 10 people buy it within a month. That was enough encouragement to keep developing it. Eventually I stopped selling it there, moved towards Steam, and dropped the web version so I wasn’t trying to support everything at once.

It has since got considerably bigger than planned. More on that mistake later 😂

**Visuals and animation**

I have a style guide which has evolved with the project: colours, textures, the overall look of things.

If I have a design in mind, I’ll sketch it on my trusty old Wacom, send it to Codex, and get some concept art based on that and the style guide using imagen. Sometimes this takes quite a few rounds before I’m happy.

From there, I send it to Claude to build in Blender. This bit requires resilience. Claude has a lot of “isms” in how it builds models, and needs quite a lot of steering to get close to the reference. Having an agreed picture of what we’re aiming for makes a massive difference.

For animations, I record myself doing the movement and get Claude to break the video into stills to use as references. Luckily the player doesn’t do anything too acrobatic. This has been particularly useful for hand animations!

**Audio**

I use Suno for music. Being able to direct the kind of track I want has worked well for me.

I’ve also used ElevenLabs for some sound effects, which has been much more hit and miss. Some outputs are very sharp or full of artifacts and need a lot of cleanup. There are still a few problem sounds in the game I want to replace before release.

That’s probably a recurring theme, generating something is quick, getting it to fit properly can take ages.

**Gameplay**

Iterate, iterate, iterate…

It’s a first-person movement game, so it lives and dies on how it feels from moment to moment.

I’ve spent a LOT of time on things like how the player collides with the world, when they should hug the floor or leave it, how much air control is too much, landing behaviour, timings of world events, map layouts, biomes and procedural generation.

I won’t pretend I fully understand every algorithm involved, but having Claude explain its constraints to my smooth brain while we work through it is useful.

AI makes it quick to try a change. I still need to play it and work out whether that change actually feels good. Sometimes something sounds sensible, passes its tests, and feels rubbish.

I’ve also been learning about “juice”, and what makes someone watch a clip and think “I have no idea what that is, but it looks cool”. This is my first game, so there’s a lot of game design learning happening alongside the development.

I am absolutely guilty of scope creep. It’s now way bigger than I originally intended, but I’m still having fun building and playing it, so apparently I haven’t learned that lesson yet.

**Fitting it around life**

I have a young family and a day job, so I need to be economical with my time.

Usually I’ll pick one or two substantial tasks, get Codex/Claude working on them in the morning, then review the results in the evening once the kids are asleep. Socials get squeezed in around that too.

This works much better when the task has a clear target and a way to check whether it’s done. Leave too much open to interpretation and Claude will just Claude.

**Mistakes and things I’m still figuring out**

* I launched the Steam page with zero marketing preparation.
* Then did much the same with the demo.
* I’m at around 500 wishlists after 3 months on Steam. Social posts can get thousands of views, but I haven’t found a reliable way to turn that into people trying or wishlisting the game.
* I’ve been using the demo almost like early access, constantly changing it based on feedback. That’s helped development, but I’m still not sure how well it works as someone’s first impression.
* I haven’t done creator outreach yet. It’s on the list, which keeps getting longer.

**What’s helped with the AI side**

* Vague goals give vague results. The more clearly I can describe what I want and how I’ll judge it, the better it goes.  Garbage in, garbage out.
* For visual work, get a reference agreed first. Trying to reach a look neither of you has pinned down is a great way to waste an evening.
* Feed screenshots of the actual game back into the concept development process. It helps new ideas fit what’s already there.
* Having both OpenAI and Anthropic tools has been useful for my workflow. I tend to use the strongest models 99% of the time.
* Tests matter. So does knowing what they actually test. I use scheduled overnight testing, but passing tests still doesn’t tell me whether a landing feels satisfying or a model looks right in motion.  So lots of play testing.

  
My background is software development, and this is my first game. A lot of my day job now is working out what I want, explaining it clearly, and checking what comes back.  The loop is exactly the same, and I’m often the slowest part of that process.

I was nervous about adding the AI disclosure because of how people might react, but I’d rather be clear about how it’s made and let people decide with that in mind.

AI has made this practical for me alongside everything else in my life. It’s also given me plenty of opportunities to discover all the things I don’t know about making games, and also helped me build the game I always wanted to exist.

There’s a free demo on the Steam page if the movement looks like your thing.

Finally, I hope this big brain dump has been useful to at least someone.
